title: Good and bad pieces

D0.outcome: Explains that a bad piece is one with few useful squares or a poor role, and that a piece can be bad now and good later.

D1.outcome: Picks the worst piece of each side in a quiet position and says why (hemmed in by its own pawns, shut out, passive).

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses among retreating, rerouting with a threat, or trading a bad piece for the opponent's best one, with a reason.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a pawn change turns a good bishop into a bad one, and which of the two bishop-and-pawn colour rules has support.

misconceptions: A bishop blocked by its own pawns is bad whatever may happen later.
Put pawns on the colour of the enemy bishop (unsupported).
conditions: A badly placed piece is first checked for a use where it stands; if it must move, it relocates with a threat; or it is exchanged for the opponent's best piece.
The rule 'with your own bishop, keep your pawns off its colour' is well supported; the rule about the enemy bishop's colour is a hypothesis.
contrasts: The bishop is hemmed in but a pawn lever frees it at once, so it is only temporarily bad.
Pawns placed on the enemy bishop's colour by the rule become targets instead.
A blocked piece on a wing where the game will not be decided.

soft_prereq_notes.OPN.NONDEV.D2: developing the bad piece is usually the first remedy
